content: Cefadroxil is a cephalosporin antibiotic that has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of specific bacterial infections. These include urinary tract infections caused by Escherichia coli, Proteus mirabilis, and Klebsiella species; skin and skin structure infections caused by Staphylococcus and/or Streptococcus species; and pharyngitis or tonsillitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci). Common side effects associated with this medication include gastrointestinal upset, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Adult Dosage and Indications 1. For uncomplicated lower urinary tract infections (e.g., cystitis), the standard dosage is 1 to 2 grams per day, which can be administered as a single daily dose or divided into two doses. 2. For other urinary tract infections, the recommended dosage is 2 grams per day, divided into two doses. 3. For skin and skin structure infections, the usual dosage is 1 gram per day, either as a single dose or divided into two doses. 4. For pharyngitis and tonsillitis caused by Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci, the dosage is 1 gram per day, given as a single dose or divided into two doses, for a duration of 10 days. Pediatric Dosage and Indications 1. For urinary tract infections in children, the recommended dosage is 30 mg/kg/day, divided into doses every 12 hours. 2. For pharyngitis, tonsillitis, and impetigo, the dosage is also 30 mg/kg/day, which can be given as a single dose or divided into two doses every 12 hours. 3. For other skin and skin structure infections, the dosage is 30 mg/kg/day, divided into two doses every 12 hours. 4. In cases of Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci infections, treatment should continue for at least 10 days. Contraindications Cefadroxil is contraindicated in patients with a known allergy to cephalosporin antibiotics. Warnings 1. Before initiating therapy, it is essential to assess the patient’s history of hypersensitivity reactions to cefadroxil, cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs. Cross-sensitivity between beta-lactam antibiotics, including cephalosporins and penicillins, has been documented and may occur in up to 10% of patients with a history of penicillin allergy. 2. If an allergic reaction occurs, the drug should be discontinued immediately. Severe hypersensitivity reactions may require emergency treatment, including epinephrine, oxygen, intravenous fluids, antihistamines, corticosteroids, pressor amines, and airway management. 3. Pseudomembranous colitis has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including cefadroxil. This condition can range from mild to life-threatening. It should be considered in patients presenting with diarrhea after antibiotic use. Mild cases may resolve with discontinuation of the drug, while moderate to severe cases may require fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, and treatment with an antibiotic effective against Clostridium difficile. Adverse Reactions 1. Gastrointestinal side effects include dyspepsia, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Pseudomembranous colitis may occur during or after treatment. 2. Allergic reactions such as rash, urticaria, angioedema, and pruritus have been reported. These typically resolve upon discontinuation of the drug. Anaphylaxis has also been observed. 3. Rare adverse effects include hepatic dysfunction (e.g., cholestasis, elevated liver enzymes), genital pruritus, vaginitis, neutropenia, fever, agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia, idiosyncratic hepatic failure, erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, serum sickness, and arthralgia. 4. Cephalosporins, including cefadroxil, have been associated with seizures, particularly in patients with renal impairment when the dosage was not adjusted. If seizures occur, the drug should be discontinued, and anticonvulsant therapy may be administered if clinically indicated. Use in Specific Populations 1. Pregnancy: Cefadroxil is classified as Pregnancy Category B by the FDA. Animal studies have not shown evidence of harm to the fetus, but there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. The drug should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. 2. Nursing Mothers: Caution is advised when administering cefadroxil to breastfeeding women. 3. Geriatric Use: Clinical studies have not identified significant differences in safety between elderly and younger patients. However, because cefadroxil is primarily excreted by the kidneys, dosage adjustments may be necessary in elderly patients with impaired renal function. 4. Renal Impairment: Dosage adjustments are required for patients with renal impairment to prevent drug accumulation. The initial dose is 1000 mg, followed by maintenance doses based on creatinine clearance rates. Pharmacokinetics Cefadroxil is rapidly absorbed after oral administration. Following single doses of 500 mg and 1000 mg, peak serum concentrations are approximately 16 mcg/mL and 28 mcg/mL, respectively. Over 90% of the drug is excreted unchanged in the urine within 24 hours. Peak urine concentrations are approximately 1800 mcg/mL after a single 500 mg dose. The drug maintains effective urinary concentrations against susceptible pathogens for 20 to 22 hours following a 1 g dose. Overdosage In cases of overdose, ingestion of less than 250 mg/kg of cephalosporins in children under six years of age is generally not associated with significant outcomes. For larger ingestions, gastric emptying may be considered. In anuric patients, approximately 63% of a 1 g oral dose can be removed during a 6 to 8-hour hemodialysis session. Storage Cefadroxil tablets should be stored at a temperature of 20° to 25°C (68° to 77°F). Brand Name Cefadroxil is marketed under the brand name Duricef.
